subject: High blood pressure
relation: is usually considered to be present when
object: a reading is 140/90 or higher taken by a healthcare professional, or 135/85 or higher taken at home.
source: NHS website: High blood pressure
source_quote: You're usually considered to have high blood pressure if your reading is: 140/90 or higher when checked by a healthcare professional 135/85 or higher when checked at home

subject: Clinic blood pressure
object: after 3 to 5 minutes of rest, with the person seated silently, legs unfolded, back supported and the arm resting at heart height.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: We recommend clinic BP is measured after 3–5 min rest, with the subject seated silently with the legs unfolded, back supported and arm resting at heart height.

subject: Blood pressure
object: at least 3 times at 1-minute intervals, and the average of the last 2 measurements recorded.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: BP should be measured at least 3 times at one-minute intervals. The average of the last 2 measurements should be recorded.

subject: In people where there is a significant difference in blood pressure between the arms,
relation: the arm with the higher measurements
object: should be used.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: In people where there is a significant difference in BP between arms, the arm with the higher measurements should be used.

subject: A blood pressure cuff
object: one made for the monitor and sized for the person: the bladder length should be 75 to 100% of the arm circumference and its width 35 to 50% of the arm circumference.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: It is important to use a cuff that is specifically made for the BP monitor and is appropriately sized for the individual . The bladder length should be 75–100% of the arm circumference and the width 35–50% of the arm circumference.

subject: People living with resistant hypertension
object: adverse cardiovascular events; a blood pressure cuff placed over clothing may overestimate blood pressure, leading to a false diagnosis of resistant hypertension.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: People living with resistant hypertension (RH) are at high risk of adverse cardiovascular events. Cuffs placed over clothing may overestimate BP, leading to a false diagnosis of RH.

subject: Blood pressure
object: many factors, including ambient noise, low temperature, stress, a full bladder, recent exercise, and caffeine or tobacco taken within the last 30 minutes.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: BP can be affected by many factors including ambient noise, low temperature, stress, full bladder, recent exercise and recent (within 30 min) ingestion of caffeine or tobacco.

subject: Semi-automatic blood pressure devices
object: people with abnormal heart rhythms, including bradycardia, frequent extrasystoles and atrial fibrillation; in these people blood pressure should be measured manually by auscultation.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Semi-automatic BP measurement devices are unreliable among people with abnormal heart rhythms including bradycardia, frequent extrasystoles and atrial fibrillation. In such individuals, manual BP measurement using auscultatory techniques should be used.

subject: If blood pressure is raised,
object: should be confirmed by ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: If the BP is raised then a diagnosis of hypertension should be confirmed by ambulatory, or home BP monitoring.

subject: A diagnosis of hypertension, and the management decisions that follow,
object: on a single occasion, because blood pressure varies markedly within an individual; a hypertensive crisis is the exception.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: A diagnosis of hypertension and subsequent management decisions should not be made on a single occasion due to marked individual BP variability , except in the context of a hypertensive crisis .

subject: For home blood pressure monitoring, people
object: record their blood pressure for 7 consecutive days, in both the morning and the evening, after appropriate training, taking 3 readings 1 minute apart each time and recording the mean of the second two.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: We advise asking people to record their BP at home for 7 consecutive days in both the morning and evening. Appropriate training should be given and people asked to take 3 readings, one minute apart, on each occasion and the mean of the second two values recorded.

subject: White coat hypertension
object: a high office or clinic blood pressure with a normal ambulatory or home blood pressure; it is more common among women and predicts developing sustained hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: White coat hypertension i.e. high office/clinic BP with normal ambulatory/home BP (Fig. 2), is more common among women and is a predictor of developing sustained hypertension and CVD.

subject: Masked hypertension
object: a normal office or clinic blood pressure with a raised ambulatory or home blood pressure; it is more common in men, smokers and people with a higher body mass index and systolic blood pressure.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Masked hypertension i.e. normal office/clinic BP with elevated ambulatory/home BP (Fig. 3), is more common in men, smokers and those with higher BMI and SBP .

subject: If masked hypertension is shown on ambulatory or home monitoring,
object: should be based on out-of-office blood pressure targets.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: If masked hypertension is demonstrated on ambulatory/home monitoring, therapeutic decisions should be based on out-of-office BP targets.

subject: In people with diagnosed white-coat hypertension,
object: should always be used to evaluate treatment.
source: Article: Faconti L, Tantirige N, Poulter NR et al. Call to action: British and Irish hypertension society position statement on blood pressure treatment thresholds and targets. Journal of Human Hypertension 2025
source_quote: * Among people with diagnosed white-coat hypertension out-of-office measurements should always be used to evaluate treatment.

subject: In people with postural symptoms or risk factors for autonomic neuropathy, such as diabetes,
object: should also be recorded lying down and standing (after at least 1 minute); postural hypotension can be considered if systolic blood pressure falls by 20 mmHg or more and/or diastolic blood pressure falls by 10 mmHg or more.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: In individuals with postural symptoms or risk factors for autonomic neuropathy (e.g. diabetes), BP should also be recorded supine and standing (after at least 1 min). A diagnosis of postural hypotension can be considered if systolic BP falls by ≥20 mmHg and/or diastolic BP falls by ≥10 mmHg .

subject: Postural hypotension
object: people with frailty, aged over 80, with multi-morbidity, type 2 diabetes or Parkinson's disease, or with symptoms; in people with postural hypotension, blood pressure should be treated to a standing target.
source: Article: Lewis P, George J, Kapil V et al. Adult hypertension referral pathway and therapeutic management: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Check for postural hypotension in those with frailty, aged >80 years, multi-morbidity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, Parkinson’s disease, or symptoms. In individuals with postural hypotension treat to a standing BP target.

subject: Primary (essential) hypertension
object: the most common form of hypertension; it has no specific, identifiable underlying cause that can be treated, and its pathophysiology is not fully understood but is thought to come from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental influences and age-related stiffening of the blood vessels.
source: Article: Clark CE, George A. Secondary hypertension for the generalist: When do you refer to hypertension specialist clinics, and how do you screen for secondary hypertension?. Clinical Medicine 2026
source_quote: Primary (essential) hypertension is the most common form of hypertension. It lacks a specific, identifiable, underlying cause amenable to intervention. Its pathophysiology is not fully understood, but is considered to result from a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental influences and age-related vascular stiffening.

subject: Secondary hypertension
object: an identifiable underlying cause or precipitating factor; it accounts for 5 to 10% of cases and may be suggested by abnormal findings when assessing for target organ damage, or by specific clinical features including characteristic symptoms, signs or demographic factors.
source: Article: Clark CE, George A. Secondary hypertension for the generalist: When do you refer to hypertension specialist clinics, and how do you screen for secondary hypertension?. Clinical Medicine 2026
source_quote: In contrast, secondary hypertension has an identifiable underlying cause or precipitating factor. It accounts for 5–10% of cases and may be suggested by abnormal findings on assessment for target organ damage (Table 3) or by specific clinical features, including characteristic symptoms, signs or demographic factors (Box 2).

subject: The chance of having high blood pressure
object: older age, having close relatives with high blood pressure, a Black African, Black Caribbean or South Asian ethnic background, an unhealthy diet (especially one high in salt), being overweight, smoking, drinking too much alcohol and feeling stressed over a long period.
source: NHS website: High blood pressure
source_quote: Things that increase your chances of having high blood pressure include: your age – you're more likely to get high blood pressure as you get older having close relatives with high blood pressure your ethnicity – you're at higher risk if you have a Black African, Black Caribbean or South Asian ethnic background having an unhealthy diet – especially a diet that's high in salt being overweight smoking drinking too much alcohol feeling stressed over a long period

subject: In England, the reported prevalence of hypertension
object: 23% in the least deprived areas, rising to 40% in the most deprived areas.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: In England, the reported prevalence of hypertension was 23% in the least deprived areas, rising to 40% in the most deprived areas .

subject: In England in 2021,
object: were reported as having hypertension, defined as a blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg or higher or taking antihypertensive medication.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: In England, 9% of young adults (aged 16–44 years) were reported as having hypertension in 2021, defined as BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg or taking antihypertensive medication .

subject: An estimated 30% of adults in the UK
object: hypertension, and at least a third of them do not reach the recommended blood pressure targets despite treatment.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: An estimated 30% of adults in the UK have hypertension, and at least 1/3rd of them fail to achieve the recommended blood pressure (BP) targets despite therapeutic intervention .

subject: Among people with young-onset hypertension,
relation: coarctation of the aorta, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome and thyroid disease
object: are rare, with a prevalence of 1% or less, whereas up to 10% may have primary hyperaldosteronism, renal artery stenosis (more commonly fibromuscular dysplasia, Takayasu arteritis or neurofibromatosis than atherosclerosis) or renal parenchymal disease.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: However, coarctation of the aorta, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing’s syndrome and thyroid disease are rare, with a prevalence among people with young-onset hypertension of 1% or less. In contrast, up to 10% may have primary hyperaldosteronism, renal artery stenosis (more commonly fibromuscular dysplasia [FMD], Takayasu arteritis or neurofibromatosis rather than atherosclerosis), or renal parenchymal disease .

subject: Secondary hypertension
object: people with apparent resistant hypertension, affecting about a third depending on the definition and clinical setting; renal diseases and primary hyperaldosteronism are the most common causes.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Secondary hypertension is common in people with apparent RH (≈1/3 subjects are affected depending on the definition and clinical setting) with renal diseases and primary hyperaldosteronism being the most common aetiologies .

subject: The indications to screen for secondary causes of hypertension
object: resistant hypertension; early-onset hypertension (before the age of 40); sudden-onset or rapidly worsening hypertension; severe hypertension (180/120 mmHg or higher); hypokalaemia on initial renal function testing; target organ damage out of proportion to the degree or duration of hypertension; and specific clinical clues such as episodic headache and palpitations, renal asymmetry, abdominal bruits or features of endocrine disease.
source: Article: Clark CE, George A. Secondary hypertension for the generalist: When do you refer to hypertension specialist clinics, and how do you screen for secondary hypertension?. Clinical Medicine 2026
source_quote: Indications to screen for secondary causes of hypertension. Resistant hypertension Early onset hypertension (age <40) Sudden onset or rapidly worsening hypertension Severe hypertension (≥180/120 mmHg) Hypokalaemia on initial renal function testing TOD out of proportion for the degree or duration of hypertension Specific clinical clues, such as episodic headache and palpitations, renal asymmetry, abdominal bruits, or features of endocrine disease

subject: Primary aldosteronism
object: the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension, with a prevalence of 2 to 6% among people with hypertension; screening should be considered in adults under 40, and where there is spontaneous or thiazide-induced hypokalaemia (serum potassium below 3.5 mmol/L), resistant hypertension, a family history or an adrenal incidentaloma found on imaging.
source: Article: Clark CE, George A. Secondary hypertension for the generalist: When do you refer to hypertension specialist clinics, and how do you screen for secondary hypertension?. Clinical Medicine 2026
source_quote: Primary aldosteronism (PA) is the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension (prevalence of 2–6% among hypertensives). Screening should be considered in adults <40 years, in the presence of spontaneous or thiazide-induced hypokalaemia (serum potassium <3.5 mmol/L), resistant hypertension, family history or adrenal incidentalomas detected on imaging.

subject: Screening for primary aldosteronism, the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension (prevalence 2 to 6% among people with hypertension),
object: measuring the plasma aldosterone-renin ratio, and hypokalaemia should be corrected before testing.
source: Article: Clark CE, George A. Secondary hypertension for the generalist: When do you refer to hypertension specialist clinics, and how do you screen for secondary hypertension?. Clinical Medicine 2026
source_quote: Primary aldosteronism (PA) is the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension (prevalence of 2–6% among hypertensives). Screening involves measurement of the plasma aldosterone–renin ratio (ARR). Hypokalaemia should be corrected before testing.

subject: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma, as causes of secondary hypertension,
object: paroxysmal or sustained hypertension, headaches, palpitations, hyperhidrosis, and non-cardiovascular symptoms such as weight loss or hypoglycaemia; the recommended investigations are plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines, with or without adrenal MRI or high-resolution CT, with or without functional imaging and/or a clonidine suppression test.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Table 5 Common causes of secondary hypertension, symptoms that raise clinical suspicion and recommended investigations. Condition | Clinical Suspicion | Investigations Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma | Paroxysmal or sustained hypertension, headaches, palpitations, hyperhidrosis, and non-CV symptoms such as weight loss or hypoglycaemia. | Plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines ± adrenal MRI/HRCT ± functional imaging and/or clonidine suppression test.

subject: Cushing syndrome, as a cause of secondary hypertension,
object: truncal obesity, striae, glucose intolerance and repeated infections; the recommended investigations are an overnight dexamethasone suppression test and a 24-hour urine free cortisol.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Table 5 Common causes of secondary hypertension, symptoms that raise clinical suspicion and recommended investigations. Condition | Clinical Suspicion | Investigations Cushing syndrome | Truncal obesity, striae, glucose intolerance and repeated infections. | Overnight dexamethasone suppression test and 24-h urine free cortisol.

subject: Obstructive sleep apnoea, as a cause of secondary hypertension,
object: snoring, daytime sleepiness, a raised body mass index or neck circumference, and a non-dipping profile on 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring; the recommended investigations are validated questionnaires such as the Epworth Sleepiness Scale or the STOP-BANG score, and an overnight oxygen saturation monitor.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Table 5 Common causes of secondary hypertension, symptoms that raise clinical suspicion and recommended investigations. Condition | Clinical Suspicion | Investigations Obstructive Sleep Apnoea | Snoring, daytime sleepiness, elevated BMI or neck circumference and non-dipping profile on 24-h ABPM. | Validated questionnaires such as Epworth Sleepiness Scale or STOP-BANG score. Overnight oxygen saturation monitor.

subject: Obstructive sleep apnoea
object: a leading yet underdiagnosed cause of secondary hypertension; it causes night-time blood pressure spikes and sustained daytime hypertension through sympathetic nerve activation from interrupted breathing.
source: Article: Clark CE, George A. Secondary hypertension for the generalist: When do you refer to hypertension specialist clinics, and how do you screen for secondary hypertension?. Clinical Medicine 2026
source_quote: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a leading yet underdiagnosed cause of secondary hypertension. It causes nocturnal BP spikes and sustained daytime hypertension due to sympathetic nerve activation from interrupted breathing.

subject: Aortic coarctation, as a cause of secondary hypertension,
object: usually asymptomatic; signs may include radio-femoral delay and lower blood pressure in the lower limbs, and the recommended investigation is MR angiography or CT of the aorta.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Table 5 Common causes of secondary hypertension, symptoms that raise clinical suspicion and recommended investigations. Condition | Clinical Suspicion | Investigations Aortic coarctation | Usually asymptomatic: signs may include radio-femoral delay and lower blood pressure in the lower extremities. | Aorta MRA/CT.

subject: Renal artery stenosis
object: resistant hypertension and/or hypertension starting at a young age, especially in women under 50; dedicated imaging (Doppler, CT or MRI) should be considered in these patients, especially with renal dysfunction (particularly on ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment), small kidney size or a history of fibromuscular dysplasia.
source: Article: Clark CE, George A. Secondary hypertension for the generalist: When do you refer to hypertension specialist clinics, and how do you screen for secondary hypertension?. Clinical Medicine 2026
source_quote: Renal artery stenosis can be associated with resistant and/or young-age onset hypertension, especially in women below the age of 50. Consider dedicated imaging (Doppler, CT or MRI) in these patients, especially if there is associated renal dysfunction (particularly with ACE-I or ARB treatment), small renal size or history of fibromuscular dysplasia.

subject: The British and Irish Hypertension Society (BIHS) criteria for routine referral
object: suspected secondary hypertension, including but not limited to hyperaldosteronism (for example with hypokalaemia); phaeochromocytoma (for example with palpitations, headache, flushing, a family history or a history of neurofibromatosis); and drug-induced hypertension (for example with a combined oral contraceptive pill or implant, hormone substitutes, steroids, NSAIDs, VEGF inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, SSNRIs, dexamphetamine or methylphenidate).
source: Article: Lewis P, George J, Kapil V et al. Adult hypertension referral pathway and therapeutic management: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Table 2 BIHS criteria for routine referrals. Suspected secondary hypertension, including, but not limited to hyperaldosteronism (e.g. hypokalaemia); phaeochromocytoma (e.g. palpitations, headache, flushing, family history, history of neurofibromatosis); drug-induced hypertension (e.g. concomitant prescription of combined oral contraceptive pill or implant, hormone substitutes, steroids, NSAIDs, VEGF inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), tricyclic antidepressants, SSNRIs, dexamphetamine, methylphenidate).

subject: Therapeutic agents and other substances that may affect blood pressure
object: cocaine, stimulants often used for ADHD, narcolepsy and hypersomnias, decongestants, bronchodilators and antidepressants (sympathetic activation); NSAIDs, sex hormones such as the combined contraceptive pill, corticosteroids, liquorice and sodium-containing antacids (volume retention); VEGF inhibitors and calcineurin inhibitors (direct vasoconstriction); and erythrocyte stimulating agents, tyrosine kinase inhibitors and diet supplements such as ephedra, yohimbine and bitter orange (other mechanisms).
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Table 3 Therapeutic agents and other substances that may affect blood pressure. Sympathetic activation | Volume retention | Direct Vasoconstriction | Other • Cocaine • Stimulants often used for ADHD, narcolepsy and hypersomnias • Decongestants • Bronchodilators • Antidepressants | • NSAIDs • Sex hormones e.g., combined contraceptive pill • Corticosteroids • Liquorice • Sodium containing antacids | • VEGF inhibitors • Calcineurin inhibitors | • Erythrocyte stimulating agents • Tyrosine kinase inhibitors • Diet supplements (Ephedra, Yohimbine, bitter orange)

subject: NSAIDs
object: the efficacy of antihypertensive drugs, so in people with resistant hypertension they should be withdrawn if no longer needed, or the minimum dose used.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: NSAIDs also lower the efficacy of antihypertensive drugs and should therefore be withdrawn in people with RH if they are no longer needed, or a minimum dose used .

subject: Combined oral contraceptives
object: a well-recognised association with hypertension, with studies showing a dose-dependent relationship with oestrogen strength; this risk is not seen with progesterone-only pills.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Hormone Therapy The association between combined oral contraceptives (CoC) and hypertension is well-recognised, with studies showing a dose-dependent relationship with oestrogen strength . This risk is not seen with Progesterone-only Pills (PoP) .

subject: Contraceptive options for women with hypertension
object: non-hormonal options, progesterone-only pills and intra-uterine devices.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Contraceptive options for hypertensive women include non-hormonal options, PoP and Intra-Uterine Devices (IUD).

subject: Corticosteroids, whether given orally, systemically or topically,
object: increase blood pressure; prednisolone below 7.5 mg daily is less likely to increase blood pressure.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Corticosteroids whether given orally, systemically or topically, may increase BP. Prednisolone below a dose of 7.5 mg daily, is less likely to increase BP .

subject: Hypertension
object: several distinct patterns of raised blood pressure, such as isolated systolic, systolic-diastolic and isolated diastolic hypertension, each with different underlying haemodynamic mechanisms; isolated systolic hypertension is the most common form of hypertension in young adults, is more common in males and in those with a higher body mass index, and its key haemodynamic feature is a raised cardiac output driven by an increased stroke volume.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Although often viewed as a single condition, hypertension encompasses several distinct patterns of BP elevation such as isolated systolic (ISH), systolic diastolic (SDH) and isolated diastolic (IDH) hypertension, each with different underlying haemodynamic mechanisms. ISH is the most common form of hypertension in young adults. It is more common in males and those with a higher BMI . Elevated cardiac output, driven by an increased stroke volume, is the key underlying haemodynamic characteristic.

subject: The pathophysiology of resistant hypertension
object: complex: inherited and environmental factors are both likely to contribute to salt and water retention, which in turn contributes to volume expansion, raised peripheral resistance and increased arterial stiffness, through the interplay of neurohormonal factors including raised aldosterone, vasopressin and sympathetic activity.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: The pathophysiology of RH is complex and both inherited and environmental factors are likely to contribute to salt and water retention, which in turn contribute to volume expansion, raised peripheral resistance and increased arterial stiffness, via the interplay of neurohormonal factors including raised aldosterone, vasopressin and sympathetic activity .

subject: High blood pressure
object: any symptoms, and many people have it without realising.

subject: Rarely, high blood pressure

subject: Albuminuria and/or haematuria in the absence of a urinary tract infection
object: renal parenchymal disease or hypertension-associated end-organ damage and should be investigated further; a formal urinary albumin:creatinine ratio is recommended as a more robust measure of albuminuria than a dipstick.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024

Formal urinary albumin: creatinine ratio (UACR) is recommended as a more robust measure of albuminuria than dipsticks.

subject: The investigations to consider for all adults with young-onset hypertension, to look for end-organ damage and assess cardiovascular risk,
object: clinic or office blood pressure; ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring; an ECG; an echocardiogram (to assess end-organ damage and coarctation of the aorta); blood tests including creatinine, eGFR, total cholesterol, triglycerides, HDL, total cholesterol to HDL ratio, LDL, non-HDL cholesterol, glucose, HbA1c and liver function; fundoscopy; height, weight and waist circumference; and an office dipstick urinalysis.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024

Investigation of EOD and assessment of cardiovascular risk (all patients) Clinic/Office BP ABPM/HBPM ECG ECHO (to assess EOD and coarctation of aorta) Blood tests to include: Creatinine, eGFR, TC, TG, HDL, TC:HDL, LDL, NHDLC, Glucose, HBA1c, Liver function (combine with those listed below) Fundoscopy Height, weight and waist circumference Office dipstick urinalysis

subject: The BIHS simplified screening protocol to exclude secondary hypertension in all people with resistant hypertension, in non-specialist settings,
object: history, symptoms, physical examination and factors affecting adherence; a blood test including kidney function, liver enzymes, full blood count, calcium and TSH; a urine dipstick; an ECG; renal imaging, such as ultrasound, to detect renal scarring and other gross abnormalities; and excluding obstructive sleep apnoea.

subject: Retinal changes
object: key to the diagnosis of malignant hypertension, so fundoscopy should be performed in all patients presenting with severely raised blood pressure, with a slit lamp and pupil dilation if necessary.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: As noted above, retinal changes are key to diagnosis of MHT and hence fundoscopic examination should be performed in all patients presenting with severely increased BP with the aid of slit lamp examination and pupillary mydriasis if necessary.

object: the risk in young people and give no information on lifetime risk.

subject: Reducing dietary salt intake to less than 5 to 6 g a day
object: all people with hypertension.

object: reducing salt by 3 grams a day lowered blood pressure by about 3.5/2 mmHg.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024

subject: Lifestyle interventions
object: all individuals with hypertension; there is a consensus on this despite the uncertainties.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Despite these uncertainties, there is a consensus that lifestyle interventions should be recommended for all individuals with hypertension .

subject: Healthy lifestyle changes that can help lower blood pressure
object: not eating too much salt (avoiding salty food or adding salt to meals), not drinking too much alcohol (avoiding more than 14 units a week on a regular basis), not drinking too much caffeine (drinks high in caffeine include coffee, tea and cola) and not smoking.
source: NHS website: High blood pressure
source_quote: Healthy lifestyle changes can help lower your blood pressure. do not eat too much salt – avoid salty food or adding salt to your meals do not drink too much alcohol – avoid drinking more than 14 alcohol units a week on a regular basis do not drink too much caffeine – drinks high in caffeine include coffee, tea and cola do not smoke

subject: A causal association between alcohol consumption and increased blood pressure
object: randomised controlled trials and Mendelian randomisation studies.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024

subject: The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, which emphasises lean proteins, whole grains, vegetables and fruits, and low-fat dairy products,
object: blood pressure in people with hypertension (systolic reduction of 11.6 mmHg) and also in people with normal blood pressure (systolic reduction of 5.3 mmHg); it is the most notable of the individual dietary strategies.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: The most notable among the individual strategies are the “ Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension ” (DASH) diet, which emphasises lean proteins, whole grains, vegetables and fruits, and low-fat dairy products . The DASH diet reduces BP in people with hypertension (SBP reduction of 11.6 mmHg) but also in normotension (SBP reduction of 5.3 mmHg) .

subject: The British and Irish Hypertension Society (BIHS)
object: starting antihypertensive drug treatment, whatever the cardiovascular disease risk, after a confirmed diagnosis of hypertension (a sustained out-of-office blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg or higher despite diet and lifestyle advice).
source: Article: Faconti L, Tantirige N, Poulter NR et al. Call to action: British and Irish hypertension society position statement on blood pressure treatment thresholds and targets. Journal of Human Hypertension 2025
source_quote: The BIHS recommend initiating pharmacological antihypertensive therapy, irrespective of cardiovascular disease risk, following a confirmed diagnosis of hypertension (sustained out-of-office BP ≥ 135/85 mmHg despite diet and lifestyle advice).

subject: Drug treatment for hypertension
object: individuals with blood pressure below 160/100 mmHg who are at moderate to high risk (established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, renal disease, or a QRISK3 score above 10%).
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Pharmacological treatment for hypertension is also recommended in individuals with BP values < 160/100 mmHg at moderate-high risk (established CVD, diabetes, renal disease, QRISK3 > 10%).

subject: In the investigation and treatment of young-onset hypertension, for people with blood pressure between 160 and 180 mmHg systolic and 100 to 120 mmHg diastolic,
object: should be started promptly.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Fig. 4 Investigation and treatment of young-onset hypertension. Among subjects with BP between 160 and 180/100–120 mmHg pharmacological interventions alongside lifestyle measures should be started promptly.

subject: In the investigation and treatment of young-onset hypertension, for people at low risk with blood pressure below 160/100 mmHg,
object: should be guided by assessment of end-organ damage: with evidence of end-organ damage, drug treatment should be started promptly; without it, lifestyle measures should be optimised, focusing on weight and reducing dietary salt and alcohol, for an interim period of 3 to 6 months.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Fig. 4 Investigation and treatment of young-onset hypertension. In subjects at low risk and with BP < 160/100 mmHg, the decision-making process should be guided by the assessment of the EOD (Table 4). In patients with evidence of EOD, pharmacological treatment should be commenced promptly. In the absence of EOD, we recommend optimisation of lifestyle measures, focusing on weight optimisation and reduction in dietary salt and alcohol for an interim period of 3 to 6 months.

subject: There are lots of different medicines for high blood pressure, and
object: depends on things like how high the blood pressure is, the person's age and their ethnicity.
source: NHS website: High blood pressure
source_quote: There are lots of different medicines for high blood pressure. The medicine recommended for you depends on things like how high your blood pressure is, your age and your ethnicity.

subject: While patients with hypertension await specialist review, for newly diagnosed patients in whom secondary causes are suspected, or aged under 40 at diagnosis, or post-partum,
relation: a drug that does not interfere with the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, such as amlodipine or an equivalent,
object: is preferred as a temporary treatment, because this makes screening tests for secondary causes of hypertension easier to interpret.
source: Article: Lewis P, George J, Kapil V et al. Adult hypertension referral pathway and therapeutic management: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: To optimise hypertension treatment whilst patients await specialist review, clinicians may wish to consider the following steps: For newly diagnosed patients in whom secondary causes are suspected, or aged <40 years at diagnosis, or post-partum, a non renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system interfering drug is preferred (e.g. amlodipine or equivalent) as a temporary treatment while awaiting specialist review. This will facilitate interpretation of screening tests for the secondary causes of hypertension.

subject: Long-acting blood pressure drugs
object: to minimise the impact of a missed dose and reduce blood pressure variability.
source: Article: Lewis P, George J, Kapil V et al. Adult hypertension referral pathway and therapeutic management: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Long acting drugs are strongly preferred to minimise the impact of a missed dose and reduce blood pressure variability.

subject: Steps 1 to 4 of the drug management of resistant hypertension
object: the A + C + D regimen is optimised, in both the choice of agents and the dose.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Steps 1–4 of the pharmacological management of RH is to ensure that the A + C + D regimen is optimised, both in terms of choice of agents and dose (Fig. 3).

subject: If blood pressure remains raised despite optimal triple therapy,
object: should be added; the classes available include alpha receptor antagonists, beta-blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and the PATHWAY-2 randomised controlled trial compared these three classes head to head and reported that spironolactone was the most effective at lowering blood pressure.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: If BP remains elevated despite optimal triple therapy, a 4th line drug should be added. There are several different drug classes available, including alpha receptor antagonists, beta-blockers and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA). The PATHWAY-2 RCT compared these three classes head-to-head and reported spironolactone was the most effective agent in lowering BP .

subject: Spironolactone
object: the only mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist licensed in the UK for resistant hypertension and should be used as the fourth-line drug of choice; it should be started at 12.5 to 25 mg once daily (if eGFR is above 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium is below 4.5 mmol/L) and can be increased to 50 mg depending on clinical response.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Spironolactone is the only MRA licensed in the UK for RH and should be used as the 4th line drug of choice. It should be initiated at 12.5–25 mg od (if eGFR > 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 and K + < 4.5 mmol/L) and can be up-titrated to 50 mg based on clinical response.

subject: The use of spironolactone
object: poor tolerability in a small number of people, such as significant hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia or erectile dysfunction in men, and menstrual irregularities and breast tenderness in women; in such situations amiloride (5 to 20 mg) can be used as an alternative.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: The use of spironolactone may be limited by poor tolerability in a small number of people, such as significant hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia or erectile dysfunction in men, and menstrual irregularities and breast tenderness in women. In such situations amiloride (5–20 mg) can be used as an alternative.

subject: In people who cannot tolerate standard doses of amlodipine because of ankle oedema,
relation: switching to a more lipophilic agent, such as lercanidipine or lacidipine,
object: may be helpful.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: In people unable to tolerate standard doses of amlodipine due to ankle oedema, switching to a more lipophilic agent - such as lercanidipine or lacidipine may be helpful .

subject: Low-dose thiazides
object: no placebo-controlled randomised trial evidence of mortality or morbidity benefit, and concerns have been raised about the risk of skin cancer with long-term use of hydrochlorothiazide, on which the MHRA has issued guidance for the UK; people need to be warned of the cancer risk and the need to avoid sun exposure, and hydrochlorothiazide should not be used in people with a history of skin cancer.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Low-dose thiazides have no placebo-controlled RCT evidence of mortality or morbidity benefits and concerns have been raised about the risk of skin cancer with long-term use of hydrochlorothiazide, and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has issued guidance on its use in the UK . People need to be warned of the cancer risk and the need to avoid sun exposure, and it should not be used in people with a history of skin cancer .

subject: The British and Irish Hypertension Society (BIHS)
object: an on-treatment blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg, or as low as reasonably achievable without causing unacceptable side effects, within 6 months of starting treatment, for all adults; possible subgroups to whom this may not apply are people who are frail and/or have limited life expectancy, where higher targets may be appropriate based on clinical judgement and the individual's tolerance of treatment.
source: Article: Faconti L, Tantirige N, Poulter NR et al. Call to action: British and Irish hypertension society position statement on blood pressure treatment thresholds and targets. Journal of Human Hypertension 2025
source_quote: The BIHS recommend an on-treatment BP target < 130/80 mmHg or as low as reasonably achievable without causing unacceptable side-effects, within 6-months of initiating treatment, for all adults. Possible subgroups to whom this may not apply are those who are frail and/or have limited life expectancy where higher targets may be appropriate based on clinical judgement and the individuals’ tolerance to treatment.

subject: The British and Irish Hypertension Society (BIHS)
object: blood pressure targets stay the same whether blood pressure is measured in the office, by a 7-day average of home readings or by a daytime average of ambulatory readings.
source: Article: Faconti L, Tantirige N, Poulter NR et al. Call to action: British and Irish hypertension society position statement on blood pressure treatment thresholds and targets. Journal of Human Hypertension 2025
source_quote: Based on this evidence, the British and Irish Hypertension Society (BIHS) recommend that BP targets remain the same whether BP is measured in the office, by 7-day average HBPM [Fig. 1] or day-time average ambulatory BP measurement (ABPM).

subject: Studies using objective measures of drugs or their metabolites in blood or urine
object: very high rates of non-adherence, around 50%, in people with apparent resistant hypertension.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Studies of non-adherence using objective measures of drugs or metabolites in blood or urine have consistently shown very high rates of non-adherence (around 50%) in people with apparent RH .

subject: The British and Irish Hypertension Society (BIHS)
object: uncontrolled clinic blood pressure (140/90 mmHg or higher) in people with confirmed raised out-of-office values (average daytime ambulatory or home blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg or higher) despite appropriate lifestyle measures and treatment with an optimal or maximum tolerated dose of at least 3 antihypertensive drugs, ideally including an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic, with both non-adherence to antihypertensive treatment and secondary causes of hypertension excluded.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: In this position statement the BIHS defines RH as uncontrolled clinic BP (≥140/90 mmHg) in people with confirmed elevated out-of-office values (average daytime ABPM or HBPM ≥ 135/85 mmHg) despite appropriate lifestyle measures and treatment with optimal (or maximum tolerated) dose of at least 3 antihypertensive drugs ideally including an ACE-I/ARB, a CCB and a thiazide-like diuretic, and exclusion of both non-adherence to antihypertensive treatment and secondary causes of hypertension (Table 1).

subject: Among treated adults with hypertension,
object: is reported as between 5% and 30%, but using the BIHS definition the estimated prevalence is more likely to be nearer 5 to 10%.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Among treated adults with hypertension the prevalence of RH is reported as between 5% and 30% . However, using the BIHS definition of RH the estimated prevalence is more likely to be nearer 5–10%.

subject: Pseudo-resistant hypertension
object: inaccurate blood pressure measurement: causes include an inaccurate device or wrong-sized cuff, the white-coat phenomenon, or marked brachial artery calcification (the Osler phenomenon), which makes the brachial artery incompressible; non-adherence to antihypertensive therapy is also a frequent cause.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Pseudo-resistant hypertension commonly results from inaccurate BP measurement. Causes include the use of an inaccurate device or wrong sized cuff, the white-coat phenomenon, or marked brachial artery calcification (Osler phenomenon) which renders the brachial artery incompressible. Non-adherence to antihypertensive therapy is a frequent cause of pseudo-resistant hypertension.

subject: If blood pressure remains above target after confirming the diagnosis of resistant hypertension, excluding pseudo-resistant hypertension and using drug and non-drug interventions,
object: should be considered.
source: Article: Faconti L, George J, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of resistant hypertension: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: If, after confirming the diagnosis of RH, excluding pseudo resistant HT and implementing pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, the BP remains above target, referral to a hypertension specialist should be considered (Fig. 1).

subject: National and international guidelines
object: adult referrals to secondary care hypertension specialists are targeted at patients in whom further investigations are likely to change management; referral is recommended as an emergency or same-day referral when patients have raised blood pressure with life-threatening target-organ damage, and as a routine referral when patients have, for example, suspected secondary hypertension, resistant hypertension or complex polypharmacy.
source: Article: Lewis P, George J, Kapil V et al. Adult hypertension referral pathway and therapeutic management: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: National and international guidelines advise that adult referrals to Secondary Care Hypertension Specialists are targeted at patients in whom further investigations are likely to change management decisions . Referrals are recommended when patients have raised blood pressure with life threatening target-organ damage (i.e. emergency/same day referrals); or when patients have, for example, suspected secondary hypertension, resistant hypertension, or complex polypharmacy (i.e. routine referrals) .

subject: The British and Irish Hypertension Society (BIHS) criteria for emergency or same-day referral
object: malignant (accelerated phase) hypertension, hypertensive crisis, and pre-eclampsia and severe hypertension in pregnancy.
source: Article: Lewis P, George J, Kapil V et al. Adult hypertension referral pathway and therapeutic management: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Table 1 BIHS criteria for emergency/same day referrals. Malignant/accelerated phase hypertension. Hypertensive crisis. Pre-eclampsia and severe hypertension in pregnancy.

subject: Before making a routine referral for hypertension, clinicians
object: that hypertension is present, by either ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring.
source: Article: Lewis P, George J, Kapil V et al. Adult hypertension referral pathway and therapeutic management: British and Irish Hypertension Society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Prior to making routine referrals, clinicians should have: Confirmed hypertension is present by either Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM) or Home Blood Pressure Monitoring (HBPM).

subject: National and international hypertension guidelines
object: adults with young-onset hypertension (aged under 40 at diagnosis) are reviewed by a hypertension specialist to exclude secondary causes of hypertension and optimise treatment.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: National and international hypertension guidelines recommend that adults with young-onset hypertension (aged <40 years at diagnosis) are reviewed by a hypertension specialist to exclude secondary causes of hypertension and optimise therapeutic regimens.

subject: Because hypertension-mediated end-organ damage is not fully reversible,
relation: prompt identification and management of people with young-onset hypertension
object: is important to reduce their increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: As hypertension-mediated EOD is not fully reversible , it is important to promptly identify and manage those with young-onset hypertension to mitigate their increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD).

subject: In cases of markedly raised blood pressure (above 180/120 mmHg),
object: is needed, and the recommendations in the BIHS guidance on the management of hypertensive crisis should be followed.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: In cases of markedly elevated BP (> 180/120 mmHg), an urgent assessment is needed and recommendations from the BIHS guidance on the management of hypertension crisis should be followed .

subject: In patients with severe hypertension without life-threatening end-organ damage,
object: should be reduced over days to weeks rather than hours, and managed with oral rather than intravenous therapy.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: In patients with severe HTN without life-threatening EOD, BP should be reduced over days to weeks, rather than hours, and managed with oral therapy rather than IV (Fig. 1 a, b, Tables 2 and 3).

subject: A hypertensive emergency
object: raised blood pressure which, if sustained over the next few hours, may lead to progressive life-threatening end-organ damage; it mainly includes conditions such as acute pulmonary oedema, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute renal failure, aortic dissection, intracerebral haemorrhage, severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, phaeochromocytoma crisis and acute coronary syndrome.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: Hypertensive emergency is elevated BP, which when sustained over the next few hours may lead to progressive life-threatening EOD. It primarily includes conditions such as acute pulmonary oedema, hypertensive encephalopathy, acute renal failure, aortic dissection, intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH), severe preeclampsia/eclampsia, pheochromocytoma crisis and acute coronary syndrome (ACS).

subject: Malignant hypertension
object: a distinct pathophysiological form of severe hypertension characterised by vascular damage from failure or loss of autoregulation of blood flow, usually in patients with chronic, uncontrolled hypertension; typically diastolic blood pressure is 120 mmHg or higher, and the clinical diagnosis requires concurrent bilateral grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy (flame or dot-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates and microaneurysms) or grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy (bilateral papilloedema), as defined by the Keith and Wagner classification.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: MHT is a distinct pathophysiological form of severe HTN characterised by vascular damage resulting from failure, or loss of autoregulation of blood flow, usually in patients with chronic, uncontrolled HTN. Typically, diastolic blood pressure (DBP) is ≥120 mmHg, and the clinical diagnosis requires concurrent bilateral grade 3 (flame or dot-shaped haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, hard exudates and microaneurysms) or grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy (bilateral papilloedema), as defined by Keith and Wagner classification.

subject: Patients with hypertensive emergencies
object: immediate attention, with management in most cases beginning in parallel with assessment; all international guidelines agree that the aim in the first 6 to 24 hours is a controlled but only partial reduction in mean arterial pressure, of no more than 20 to 25% and usually a fall in diastolic blood pressure of 10 to 15% or to about 110 mmHg, while aiming to keep diastolic blood pressure above 100 mmHg except in acute aortic syndromes.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: Patients with hypertensive emergencies need immediate attention and, in most cases, the management should begin parallel with assessment. Overall, there is an agreement in all international guidelines that the aim in the first 6–24 h is a controlled but only partial reduction of the MAP: no more than 20–25% and usually a fall in DBP of 10–15% or to ~110 mmHg, whilst aiming to maintain the DBP above 100 mmHg except in acute aortic syndromes.

subject: In chronic hypertension, cerebral autoregulation
object: to higher mean arterial pressures, so organs cannot compensate for a sudden fall in pressure below the new lower limit of autoregulation, and in malignant hypertension autoregulation itself is impaired; this means that lowering blood pressure to low values can compromise blood flow to vital organs.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: In chronic HTN the cerebral autoregulation is shifted upwards, i.e., to higher MAP levels, meaning that organs cannot compensate for a sudden fall in pressure below the new lower level of autoregulation , and in MHT, autoregulation itself is impaired . This means that lowering BP to low values, can compromise blood flow to vital organs.

subject: For patients with hypertensive emergencies, who need immediate attention with management in most cases beginning in parallel with assessment,
object: mainly includes labetalol (a combined alpha and beta blocker), which is commonly used first line, especially in hypertensive encephalopathy, intracerebral haemorrhage and aortic dissection, along with vasodilators.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: Patients with hypertensive emergencies need immediate attention and, in most cases, the management should begin parallel with assessment. Overall, choice of antihypertensive agents (Fig. 1c, Tables 2 – 13) mainly includes labetalol (combined α and β blocker) which is commonly used as a first line agent, especially in hypertensive encephalopathy, ICH, and aortic dissection along with vasodilators.

subject: By far the safest management of uncomplicated malignant hypertension
object: oral rather than intravenous therapy, unless there is a co-existent emergency condition or hypertension multi-organ damage.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: By far the safest management of uncomplicated MHT (Fig. 1c, Fig. 2) is oral therapy rather than IV therapy unless there is a co-existent emergency condition or hypertension multi-organ damage .

subject: The BIHS position on managing malignant (accelerated) hypertension
object: in uncomplicated malignant hypertension (eye changes alone) blood pressure is to be lowered within days, aiming for a gradual reduction to reach target blood pressure within weeks: for example, below 200/120 mmHg within 24 hours, below 160/100 mmHg within a week, then below 140/90 mmHg within 6 to 12 weeks.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: Table 4 BIHS position: Management of malignant hypertension (MHT)/accelerated hypertension. In uncomplicated MHT (eye changes alone) BP is to be lowered within days, aiming for gradual reduction to reach target BP within weeks. For example: within 24 h lower to <200/120 mmHg, within a week <160/100 mmHg, then to <140/90 mmHg within 6–12 weeks.

subject: For patients presenting with malignant hypertension
object: no definite evidence on the medication of choice; calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine 5 mg or long-acting (12 to 24 hour) nifedipine 10 to 30 mg, or a low-dose beta blocker such as atenolol 25 mg, may be reasonable first choices if suspicion of an underlying phaeochromocytoma is low, and it is crucial not to use short-acting nifedipine.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Glover M, Kapil V et al. Management of hypertensive crisis: British and Irish Hypertension Society Position document. Journal of Human Hypertension 2022
source_quote: There is no definite evidence regarding medication of choice for patients presenting with MHT. Calcium channel blockers (CCB) such as amlodipine 5 mg or nifedipine long acting (12–24 h) 10–30 mg, or a low dose β blocker such as atenolol 25 mg may be reasonable first choices if suspicion of an underlying phaeochromocytoma is low. It is crucial, not to use short acting formulation nifedipine.

subject: In the investigation and treatment of young-onset hypertension, among women of childbearing potential
object: plans for future pregnancy and contraception use and, where appropriate, the potential harmful effects of ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists in pregnancy; an informed decision can then be made about whether drugs that can be routinely used during pregnancy (such as modified-release nifedipine, amlodipine or beta blockers) should be used in place of drugs that block the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
source: Article: Kulkarni S, Faconti L, Partridge S et al. Investigation and management of young-onset hypertension: British and Irish hypertension society position statement. Journal of Human Hypertension 2024
source_quote: Fig. 4 Investigation and treatment of young-onset hypertension. Among women of childbearing potential it is important to discuss plans for future pregnancy and contraception use and, where appropriate, the potential detrimental effects of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin II receptor antagonists in pregnancy. An informed decision can then be made about whether drugs that can be routinely used during pregnancy (such as modified release nifedipine, amlodipine or beta blockers) should be used in place of RAAS-blocking drugs .

subject: Blood pressure that is too high
object: extra strain on the blood vessels, heart and other organs such as the brain, kidneys and eyes; if not treated, it can increase the risk of serious conditions such as heart disease, heart attacks, strokes, heart failure, kidney disease and vascular dementia.

If it's not treated, it can increase your risk of serious conditions such as: heart disease heart attacks strokes heart failure kidney disease vascular dementia

subject: High blood pressure
object: the leading modifiable risk factor for premature morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular disease worldwide, and contributes significantly to chronic kidney disease, heart failure and dementia.
source: Article: Faconti L, Tantirige N, Poulter NR et al. Call to action: British and Irish hypertension society position statement on blood pressure treatment thresholds and targets. Journal of Human Hypertension 2025
source_quote: High blood pressure (BP) is the leading modifiable risk factor for premature morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular disease (CVD) worldwide, and significantly contributes to chronic kidney disease, heart failure and dementia .

subject: The Blood Pressure Lowering Treatment Trialists' Collaboration
object: the reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events was proportional to the size of the fall in systolic blood pressure, down to at least 120 mmHg in people aged under 75, with and without previous cardiovascular disease; overall, events were reduced by 10% for each 5 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure, with a greater effect in younger people (aged under 55: hazard ratio 0.82, 95% confidence interval 0.76 to 0.88) than in older people (aged 65 to 74: hazard ratio 0.91, 95% confidence interval 0.87 to 0.96).
source: Article: Faconti L, Tantirige N, Poulter NR et al. Call to action: British and Irish hypertension society position statement on blood pressure treatment thresholds and targets. Journal of Human Hypertension 2025
source_quote: The Blood Pressure Lowering Treatment Trialists’ Collaboration reported that the reduction in MACE was proportional to the magnitude of the fall in SBP down to at least 120 mmHg in those aged < 75 years, with and without prior cardiovascular disease . Overall, MACE was reduced by 10% per 5 mmHg reduction in Systolic BP (SBP), with a greater effect in younger (age <55 years: HR 0·82 [95% CI: 0·76–0·88]) compared with older individuals (age 65–74 years: HR 0·91 [95%CI: 0·87–0·96]) .
